<reason>Both sides argued at a high level with disciplined, non-fabricated reasoning, but PRO built the cleaner path to a vote on the motion as written. PRO's frame — access to essentials should not rest on corporate discretion, and a floor is set before it gives way ("the fire exit changes nothing until the fire") — squarely answered CON's central weighing claim that the mandate "changes nothing" for today's excluded shoppers. PRO also largely defused CON's deleted-store mechanism by pointing out that acceptance requires a bill-taking terminal, not a payroll, technology chains already run. CON's strongest work was exposing the "stock that shelf with non-essentials" fallback as an admitted deletion and pressing the benefit-card point, but CON's cost case remained a hypothesis about unbuilt formats in unnamed places (which CON honestly admitted), while its financial-inclusion alternative was credibly characterized as a decades-long promise. CON's closing move that the mandate "puts no bill in anyone's wallet" partly dodged the resilience argument, which is about stores being able to take cash people already hold. A competitive but real PRO edge.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The A1 exchange after Pressure Questions: PRO answered "covered" and swapped the cashier for cash-accepting machines, undercutting CON's staffing-based deletion story; CON struck back sharply by seizing PRO's "stock non-essentials" fallback as the deleted store in PRO's own words. PRO's closing reply that no chain would abandon the essentials market over one terminal it already runs elsewhere kept the mechanism mostly neutralized.</best_rebuttal>
